title: The Real Cancun
full_review:
Every once in a while a movie is so utterly inane that to dignify it with a review seems to compound its absurdity by somehow deeming it worthy of analysis. Such is "The Real Cancun" (New Line) -- a film which gives credence to 20th-century Irish playwright St. John Ervine's assessment that most American movies are created "by the half-educated for the half-witted."

The film's producers, Mary-Ellis Bunim and Jonathan Murray, who helped define the reality TV genre back in 1987 with MTV's "The Real World," unabashedly admit that "Cancun" offers viewers "something they don't get on television, which is, quite frankly, some nudity, some sexual situations and language that is more realistic" -- crude -- "and honest." Such brazen exploitation and pandering to the lowest common denominator by the media elite, while increasingly prevalent, is disconcerting and symptomatic of a much deeper societal decay.

In a nutshell, 16 college students are set loose in a private wing of beachfront suites in Cancun, Mexico, during spring break. Following the rules of the faux genre, the rooms are rigged with cameras and microphones to record their every move, conversation and wet T-shirt contest. What follows is little more than an eight-day chronicle of drunken frat-house debauchery and hedonistic promiscuity. The promotion of casual sex and inebriation is exacerbated by the banality of the intoxicated cast members' incessant banter.

The bacchanalia includes Roxanne and Nicole, Texan twins whose bodies are developed in direct disproportion to their sense of self-dignity; Jeremy, a sexual athlete from Arizona State with a steroid-inflated ego; and Alan, the quintessential "good boy" who is applauded for ultimately succumbing to peer pressure.

To summarize the "plot" any further would presuppose that a modicum of mental effort was involved in the production of this mindless dreck, a dangerous assumption. It would also lend far too much credibility to an execrable pastiche of raunchy vulgarities and lewd excesses, slickly packaged and marketed and fatuously passed off as some sort of pseudo, Gen-Y cinema verite.

The French philosopher-novelist Albert Camus once observed that future historians would only know two things about modern man: "that he read newspapers and fornicated." This film, if viewed by those future historians, would only prove the existentialist half-correct -- no one reads newspapers in "The Real Cancun."

While "The Real Cancun" hardly signals the death knell of Western civilization, anyone foolish enough to consider plopping down cash to see this smut would be advised to heed the advice of Alfred Hitchcock: "If you want reality, sit outside the theater."

Due to a glamorizing attitude toward casual sex, recurring raunchy sexual situations with nudity, incessant alcohol abuse, excessive rough language, as well as vulgarities and lewd, sexually explicit language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
